title: Lawsuit: Amazon refused to give pregnant workers bathroom breaks and chairs
gist: Four former Amazon warehouse workers filed a nationwide class-action lawsuit alleging Amazon systematically denied pregnancy accommodations (bathroom breaks, chairs, lifting limits) required under the 2022 Pregnant Workers Fairness Act and then fired them via its attendance policy after they used medical leave, backed by an EEOC finding of reasonable cause against Amazon; Amazon disputes the claims and says it approves 99.9% of pregnancy accommodation requests.

insights.claim: Four former Amazon warehouse workers (Willamina Barclay, Kristina Green, Jennifer Hatch, Dazaria Parks) filed a nationwide class-action lawsuit in the US District Court for the Eastern District of New York alleging Amazon denied basic pregnancy accommodations like bathroom breaks, an extra 15-minute break, and sitting instead of standing.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: A nationwide class action against the largest US private employer over PWFA compliance creates exposure to significant back-pay, benefits, and punitive-damages liability if certified.
insights.quote: Amazon denied them basic modifications the law recognizes pregnant workers regularly need, even in uncomplicated pregnancies: Bathroom breaks. An extra 15-minute break. Sitting instead of standing.
insights.locator: said the lawsuit filed in US District Court

insights.claim: The lawsuit leans on the 2022 federal Pregnant Workers Fairness Act (PWFA), which requires employers to provide reasonable accommodations for pregnancy-related conditions absent undue hardship, giving plaintiffs a newer and more specific legal basis than prior discrimination claims against Amazon.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: The PWFA is a relatively new, still-being-tested statute; how this case proceeds will help calibrate future PWFA litigation risk for large employers with physically demanding warehouse roles.
insights.locator: this one has the added backing of a 2022 US law

insights.claim: In February 2026 the EEOC found reasonable cause that Amazon discriminated against a nationwide class of female warehouse associates based on pregnancy by failing to accommodate them, and issued plaintiff Jennifer Hatch a Notice of Right to Sue on August 26, 2026.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: A federal agency reasonable-cause finding materially strengthens plaintiffs' position ahead of litigation or settlement and is a meaningful signal of regulatory risk for Amazon's labor practices.
insights.locator: The US Equal Employment Opportunity Commission

themes.theme: Alleged mechanism: attendance policy as retaliation

insights.claim: The lawsuit alleges Amazon's Punitive Attendance Policy converted medically necessary breaks and absences into deductions from a limited bank of unpaid time off, and once that bank was depleted, workers were fired — effectively penalizing pregnancy-related medical needs through a facially neutral attendance system.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: This is the structural mechanism at the heart of the case: an attendance-point system that doesn't explicitly target pregnancy can still produce disparate termination outcomes, a pattern plaintiffs' attorneys can generalize to other protected classes.
insights.quote: Amazon deducted their limited bank of unpaid time off. Soon enough, they had depleted that limited bank of ‘unpaid time off,’ and Amazon threatened to terminate them.
insights.locator: took medically necessary breaks or absences

insights.claim: Amazon allegedly required medical documentation for even basic pregnancy accommodation requests, despite EEOC 2024 guidance stating that documentation is not reasonable to demand for a small set of commonly needed modifications like water access, extra bathroom breaks, and sitting while working.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: A documented gap between EEOC guidance and Amazon's internal accommodation policy is exactly the kind of evidence that can support both the class-wide claim and individual damages.
insights.locator: Amazon applied its unlawful policy of demanding medical paperwork

insights.claim: Amazon states that in the past year it approved more than 99.9 percent of pregnancy-related accommodation requests, including additional breaks, modified duty, or seated roles, and offers up to 20 weeks of fully paid leave for eligible birthing parents.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin (quoting Amazon statement)
insights.so_what: Amazon's aggregate approval-rate defense will likely be a central plank of its response strategy; investors should watch whether the 99.9% figure is challenged or substantiated as the case proceeds.
insights.quote: In the past year, more than 99.9 percent of pregnancy related accommodations requests have been approved

insights.claim: This lawsuit follows a similar October 2025 suit by the state of New Jersey against Amazon alleging widespread discrimination against pregnant workers and employees with disabilities, indicating a pattern of recurring legal exposure on this issue.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Multiple independent legal actions (a state AG suit plus a federal class action) on the same fact pattern raise the probability this becomes a costly, recurring legal/reputational liability rather than an isolated incident.
insights.locator: The state of New Jersey previously sued Amazon

insights.claim: Amazon reported $200.6 billion in net sales and $62.6 billion in net income for Q2 2026, context cited alongside the discrimination allegations.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Establishes the financial scale against which any eventual settlement, fine, or punitive damages award would be assessed — likely immaterial to Amazon's overall financials even at significant settlement size.
insights.locator: Amazon reported $200.6 billion in net sales in Q2 2026
